reader.summary: The week was dominated by the deliberate car-ramming attack on Australian MP Helen Haines, who lost both legs and whose attacker was charged with a targeted assault. Police called the incident deliberate, the PM said it was 'no accident,' and a terrorism squad opened an inquiry. A second female lawmaker was threatened days later, and coverage highlighted a growing pattern of threats against Australian politicians. In sport, South Africa beat Australia by an innings in the second Test to level the series 1-1, leaving Australia with selection headaches ahead of the Cape Town decider. New Zealand won the second Bledisloe test 43-21, while Australia's women's rugby league team thrashed England 78-0 in the World Cup. Economically, the RBA warned the inflation outlook was 'materially worse' while noting labour-market easing, and growth is likely to slow. Shares in Zip fell 50% after a fraud incident, and data-centre operator NextDC dropped over 40% on an earnings warning. The Snowy Hydro project's cost blew out to an estimated $18 billion, eleven times the original estimate. Meta and TikTok faced new Australian lawsuits over harm to children, and a review found KPMG Australia mishandled whistleblower claims. China's appetite for Australian canola picked up as trade ties improved, while iron-ore and bauxite miners warned of production risk without a China deal. One contradiction: the Financial Times described Sydney's second airport as a 'long haul' while Bloomberg reported the $4 billion airport opening with barely any flights.

display.eli5:
Last week, an Australian politician named Helen Haines was deliberately run over by a car and lost both legs. A second female politician was also threatened. Police say it was on purpose, and a special terrorism team is looking into why. Next week, the person who drove the car will go to court for a bail hearing, and police will start a proper investigation into the second threat.

The reason this is a big deal is that Australian politicians have been getting more and more threats lately, and this was the worst one yet. The prime minister called it 'no accident,' which means the government is taking it very seriously.

In cricket, Australia and South Africa are tied in a best-of-three series. The deciding match is in Cape Town, and Australia is in a mess because their best player got hurt and they need to pick a new team. Expect a dramatic result either way.

In the economy, the central bank said prices are getting worse than expected, and big companies are cutting jobs and lowering their profit forecasts. This means the stock market is nervous.

A surprise would be if the stock exchange itself announces a formal investigation into the computer glitches that happened this week, or if the government suddenly announces new security rules for all politicians.
